lead: A total station is an electronic theodolite with an EDM and a processor in one instrument. It measures horizontal angle, vertical angle and slope distance to a prism at one setup, then computes coordinates. It exists because separate theodolite, tape and calculator work is slow and error-prone on a busy site. You see it in topographic surveys, road and building setting out, cadastral work, tunnel control and deformation monitoring. Some syllabi call it an electronic tacheometer.
prereq: You need: EDM from the foundations of surveying and the theodolite; setting out in 5.6 reverses the coordinate step.

blocks.text: A total station does three jobs in one body: an electronic theodolite measures angles, an EDM measures distance to a reflector prism, and a processor combines them. The telescope rotates about a horizontal axis (the trunnion axis); the whole upper assembly, carrying that axis, rotates about the vertical axis of the instrument. The tribrach levels the instrument and centres it over the station mark. A display and keypad run menus; a battery powers the set; storage holds raw angles, distances and coordinates. Angles are quoted in degrees, minutes and seconds: 1° = 60′ (minutes of arc) = 3600″ (seconds of arc).

items: Horizontal and vertical angle encoders read the circles electronically, often to 1″ or better.
The EDM unit measures the phase difference of a modulated light beam sent to the prism and back; it gives slope distance S.
The reflector prism returns the beam. Its prism constant is the small offset between the optical centre and the mechanical mounting, entered with its sign.
An optical or laser plummet centres the instrument over the ground mark.
The processor applies the prism constant and atmospheric correction, then computes horizontal distance and coordinates.

blocks.where: d is horizontal distance in metres; S is the corrected slope distance in metres (after prism constant); z is the zenith angle in degrees, measured from the vertical.

blocks.text: A motorized total station turns under keypad control. A robotic total station follows the prism and lets one person survey alone.

items: Set the tripod over the station, mount the instrument, and level with the foot screws.
Centre the station mark under the plummet while keeping the bubble centred. Forced centring is better on control surveys.
Enter station coordinates, height of instrument HI, and target height HT.
Sight the backsight, enter its azimuth or coordinates, and set the horizontal circle. This orientation fixes the direction of the survey.
Turn to the target. Read horizontal angle β clockwise from the backsight, zenith angle z, and slope distance S.

Correct the slope distance first: S<sub>c</sub> = S + k, where k is the prism constant in metres with its sign. Then compute d = S<sub>c</sub> sin z and ΔV = S<sub>c</sub> cos z. The target reduced level is RL<sub>target</sub> = RL<sub>station</sub> + HI + ΔV − HT.

blocks.text: E<sub>R</sub> = E<sub>P</sub> + d sin A     N<sub>R</sub> = N<sub>P</sub> + d cos A
blocks.where: E and N are easting and northing in metres; P is the station; R is the target; d is horizontal distance in metres; A is the azimuth of the line in degrees, clockwise from north, given by A = azimuth of backsight + β; β is the clockwise horizontal angle turned from the backsight.

blocks.text: The processor repeats this for every shot. Stakeout reverses it: enter a design point and the display shows the angle to turn and the distance to measure. Field work covers traversing, topographic detail, as-built surveys and setting out. Prismless EDM suits short ranges to walls or rock faces. Transfer data by USB or Bluetooth.
Every error enters the coordinates through an angle or a distance.

items: Collimation error: the line of sight is not square to the horizontal axis. It makes horizontal angles wrong; check by reversing the telescope.
Vertical index error: the vertical circle zero is mis-set. It tilts heights and horizontal distance through z; check face left and face right.
Circle eccentricity: the circle centre is not on the axis. The error varies with angle; modern instruments correct it.

Prism constant wrong: every slope distance shifts by the full prism constant k; horizontal distance shifts by k sin z and the height difference by k cos z. A 30 mm slip ruins stakeout even when it looks small.
Centring, HI and HT errors: a wrong station position, height of instrument or target height shifts coordinates or levels. Measure HI and HT with a tape.
Atmosphere and refraction: temperature and pressure change light speed; enter corrected values. Hot ground bends the line of sight near the surface.
Booking errors: wrong point name, angle mode or sign. Record raw data and check the first few coordinates.

blocks.text: For monitoring, repeat the same setup and check fixed reference points.

spec.aria: Plan with station P, backsight Q at azimuth 30 degrees and the target R at azimuth 105 degrees 30 minutes, 119.543 metres away; side view with the slope distance, horizontal distance, vertical component, instrument and target heights and the reduced level of R, 35.209 metres.

examples.question: At station P (E 1000.000 m, N 2000.000 m), backsight Q has azimuth 30°00′00″. A total station reads a clockwise horizontal angle β = 75°30′00″ from PQ to R, a slope distance of 120.000 m and a zenith angle of 85°00′00″. Find the horizontal distance PR, the azimuth of PR, and the coordinates of R.
steps: Prism constant is zero here, so S<sub>c</sub> = S = 120.000 m. Horizontal distance: d = S<sub>c</sub> sin z = 120.000 × sin 85° = 120.000 × 0.996195 = 119.543 m.
Easting difference: ΔE = d sin A = 119.5434 × 0.963630 = 115.196 m (keep d unrounded until the end).
Northing difference: ΔN = d cos A = 119.5434 × (−0.267238) = −31.947 m.

examples.question: From the same station P (E 1000.000 m, N 2000.000 m, RL 25.000 m), with the circle oriented on the backsight Q at azimuth 30°00′00″, the instrument height is 1.550 m. (a) The shot to R in the first example had S = 120.000 m and z = 85°00′00″ with a target height of 1.800 m: find the reduced level of R. (b) A design point D at (E 1050.000 m, N 2080.000 m) is to be staked out: find the angle to turn from the backsight and the horizontal distance to lay out.
steps: Vertical component of the shot to R: ΔV = S cos z = 120.000 × cos 85° = 120.000 × 0.087156 = 10.459 m.
Reduced level of R: RL<sub>R</sub> = RL<sub>P</sub> + HI + ΔV − HT = 25.000 + 1.550 + 10.459 − 1.800 = 35.209 m.
Stake-out of D: ΔE = 1050.000 − 1000.000 = +50.000 m and ΔN = 2080.000 − 2000.000 = +80.000 m, so D lies north-east of P.
Azimuth PD = tan⁻¹(50.000/80.000) = tan⁻¹ 0.625 = 32°00′19″ (first quadrant, both differences positive).
Angle to turn clockwise from the backsight: 32°00′19″ − 30°00′00″ = 2°00′19″.
In the field the display shows the remaining angle and distance as the prism is moved; the peg is driven when both read zero, then the point is measured again as a check.
examples.answer: RL of R = 35.209 m. To set out D, turn 2°00′19″ clockwise from the backsight and lay out 94.340 m horizontally.

traps: Using slope distance S as horizontal distance; you must multiply by sin z.
Forgetting the prism constant, or entering it with the wrong sign, so every distance is offset.
Ignoring height of instrument HI or target height HT when reducing levels.
Turning the wrong way: β is clockwise from the backsight, and A is clockwise from north.
Skipping the atmospheric correction on long sights, then blaming the instrument for a small scale error.

quiz.q: Name three main parts of a total station and state the job of each.
quiz.a: EDM unit measures slope distance to a prism; angle encoders read horizontal and vertical angles; processor computes distances and coordinates.
The small offset between the prism optical centre and its mechanical mounting, entered in the instrument and applied to measured distance.

quiz.q: Why must a total station be oriented on a backsight before measuring new points?
quiz.a: The instrument needs a known reference direction. The backsight azimuth or coordinates set the horizontal circle, so measured clockwise angles become azimuths and computed coordinates are in the survey grid.

quiz.q: Station P is at E 500.000 m, N 600.000 m. A shot has slope distance 200.000 m, zenith angle 80°00′00″ and azimuth 120°00′00″. Find horizontal distance, ΔE, ΔN and the coordinates of the target.
A 10 mm error is made in height of instrument HI. Which results change: horizontal coordinates or reduced levels? Explain.
quiz.a: Only reduced levels change, by 10 mm, because HI enters RL<sub>target</sub> = RL<sub>station</sub> + HI + ΔV − HT. Horizontal coordinates use horizontal distance and azimuth, not HI.

quiz.q: A prism constant of 30 mm is left out on a 500.000 m slope distance with zenith angle 85°. Estimate the horizontal distance error.
quiz.a: The slope distance is short by 0.030 m. Horizontal error ≈ 0.030 sin 85° = 0.0299 m, about 30 mm; all computed coordinates shift by this amount along the sight.

beyond: Not for the exam. Robotic total stations now add motorized tracking, imaging and scan modes, and they feed coordinates straight into stakeout software and BIM models. Monitoring firms run total stations on fixed piers with automatic repeat cycles for dams, bridges and metro tunnels. Search for robotic total station stakeout, prism constant sign, reflectorless EDM accuracy, and total station monitoring systems.
